newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court strikes down state charity tax law.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court strikes down state charity tax law.

text.p: A divided Supreme Court ruled Monday that states and local governments may not deprive charity groups of property tax exemptions if they operate mainly to benefit out-of-state residents.
The high court, by a 5-4 vote, struck down a Maine law on the grounds that it violates the constitutional protections against discrimination in interstate commerce.

"States are not free to levy such taxes in a manner that discriminates against interstate commerce," Justice John Paul Stevens declared for the court majority. He said there is no question the tax would be unconstitutional if it targeted profit-making entities.
The ruling represented a victory for Camps Newfound/Owatonna, which appealed its 1989-91 property tax bill of more than $20,000 a year from the town of Harrison.
All but five percent of its campers come from outside Maine, which made it ineligble for the exemption that otherwise would apply to charity groups incorporated within the state.
The high court decision had been expected as the justices in their last term struck down a North Carolina property tax that operated in a similar fashion.
Charity and religious groups urged the high court to strike down the Maine law on the grounds that it threatens more than two centuries of tax exemptions for religious charities.

"It will be open season on the skimpy coffers of charities nationwide. We can expect revenue-hungry states and cities to tax all but the smallest of charities," Steven McFarland of the Christian Legal Society's Center for Law and Religious Freedom, said, in warning what would happen if the law were upheld.
In dissent, Justice Antonin Scalia said states should be free to give tax breaks to charities that benefit state's residents.

He warned the ruling may have broad implications, saying a state must give a tax exemption to private schools serving both in-state and out-of-state residents and to a charity with the main purpose of feeding the poor of another nation.
In other action Monday, the Supreme Court:
-- ruled unanimously that the secretary of transportation has the authority to name civilian judges to the Coast Guard Court of Criminal Appeals, and that the appointments are constitutionally valid.

-- agreed to decide in its term starting in October whether a military rule barring polygraph evidence in court-martial proceedings unconstitutionally infringes on a defendant's right to present a defense.

-- agreed to decide the constitutionality of a New York law which gives residents, but not nonresidents, a full deduction from state income tax liability for alimony payments. The law had been challenged in court as a form for discriminating against nonresidents.

-- unanimously ruled that an inmate in Washington state cannot proceed with a civil rights complaint over a disciplinary hearing because the prisoner failed to seek the restoration of 30 days of lost good-time credit.
-- let stand a ruling that California must hire as a plant inspector at the border a Seventh Day Adventist who refused for religious reasons to work on Saturday.
